# Bar graphs {#sec-bar-graphs} :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false} ::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** :::
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bar_graphs_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: :::: ## Description A bar graph compares data in different categories using rectangular bars that vary in length or height. They can be vertical or horizontal, with the vertical axis showing the quantities being measured and the horizontal axis listing the categories. Bar graphs often include a legend explaining the colors or patterns used when comparing multiple variables. In `ggplot2`, bar graphs can be built using [`geom_bar()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html). ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} install.packages("palmerpenguins") library(palmerpenguins) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: ::: {.column-margin} ![Artwork by Allison Horst](www/lter_penguins.png){fig-align="right" width="65%"} ::: Filter the missing values from `species` in the `palmerpenguins::penguins` data and store it in `penguins_bar`. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} penguins_bar <- palmerpenguins::penguins |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(species)) glimpse(penguins_bar) #> Rows: 344 #> Columns: 8 #> $ species Adelie, Adelie, Adelie… #> $ island Torgersen, Torgersen, … #> $ bill_length_mm 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, … #> $ bill_depth_mm 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, … #> $ flipper_length_mm 181, 186, 195, NA, 193… #> $ body_mass_g 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, … #> $ sex male, female, female, … #> $ year 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007… ``` ::: ::: ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: 1. Create labels with `labs()` 2. Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` 3. Map `species` to the `x` axis 4. Map `species` to the `fill` aesthetic inside the `aes()` of `geom_bar()` 5. Remove the legend with `show.legend = FALSE` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_bar <- labs( title = "Adult foraging penguins", subtitle = "Distribution of flipper length", x = "Species", y = "Count", fill = "Species") ggp2_bar <- ggplot(data = penguins_bar, aes(x = species)) + geom_bar(aes(fill = species), show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_bar + labs_bar ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bar_graphs_files/figure-html/create_graph_bar-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ## More info The connection between statistical transformations and geoms is an important principle for building graphs (and mastering the grammar) with `ggplot2`. Below we cover why `geom_bar(stat = "count")` produces the same result as `stat_count(geom = "bar")`.[^geom-bar] ::: {.column-margin} "*every geom has a default stat, and every stat a default geom.*" - [`ggplot2` book](https://ggplot2-book.org/layers.html#layers) ::: [^geom-bar]: Bar graphs can also be created with [`geom_col()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html#ref-examples) ### Stats and geoms ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **stat_count():** ::: The default `stat` argument in `geom_bar()` is set to `"count"`, which '*counts the number of cases at each `x` position*', so it's ideal for categorical variables (or factors). The `stat_count()` function can also be used to create bar graphs using the `geom` argument. The link between `geom_`**geom_name**`(stat = "`**stat_name**`")` and `stat_`**stat_name**`(geom = "`**geom_name**`")` is shown below: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_geom_bar <- ggplot(data = penguins_bar, aes(x = species)) + geom_bar(aes(fill = species), stat = "count") + labs(title = "geom_bar(stat = 'count')") ggp2_geom_bar ggp2_stat_count <- ggplot(data = penguins_bar, aes(x = species)) + stat_count(aes(fill = species), geom = "bar") + labs(title = "stat_count(geom = 'bar')") ggp2_stat_count ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bar_graphs_files/figure-html/stat_vs_geom_bar-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bar_graphs_files/figure-html/stat_vs_geom_bar-2.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `geom_col()` ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **geom_col():** ::: To create a bar graph with `geom_col()`, the `count` variable needs to be computed before being mapped into the graph `y` aesthetic. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins_bar |> # create column of counts dplyr::count(species, name = "count") |> # map into x and y ggplot(mapping = aes(x = species, y = count)) + geom_col(aes(fill = species), show.legend = FALSE) + labs_bar + labs(caption = "*geom_col()") # compare to geom_bar() ggp2_bar + labs_bar ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bar_graphs_files/figure-html/bar_with_geom_col-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](bar_graphs_files/figure-html/bar_with_geom_col-2.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: :::
